title: Knowing God: The Trinity and the Life It Makes Possible
subtitle: A five-session study on the God who is three-in-one, and the life that knowing him makes possible.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have studied God for years and quietly suspect they have never met him, and for those who came to the church for a system to believe and found a doctrine called the Trinity that sounded like a math problem no one could solve. It walks through the oldest confession the church holds, that the one God is eternally three persons, Father, Son, and Spirit, and asks the question underneath all theology, whether the point of any of it was ever to be right about God or to know him. Not a book about God. A slow walk toward the God who is there. The difference between studying him and being acquainted with him, and the danger of theology that never becomes prayer. The doctrine of the Trinity stated carefully and historically, not as a puzzle to crack but as the reason God can be called love. The Father who runs toward the returning child. The Son who is the exact imprint of God's nature, so that the God who could have stayed unknown made himself known. And the Spirit who does not leave us studying God from across a room but draws us inside the love that the Father and the Son have had forever.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a diagram of God to file away. It will refuse that, and the leader must refuse it too. The Trinity is not a problem to be solved. It is the name of the God who saved us, and to know him is the whole of eternal life. Some in the room have spent years acquiring facts about God and have never once been sure they were known by him. Bell knows that pew. He came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith and a trained suspicion of every claim about the divine, and he had to learn the difference between an argument that convinced him God exists and a Father who knew his name. He is not standing outside this study explaining God to people who find him distant. He spent years finding him distant. He writes from inside the long walk from knowing about God to knowing him, and the leader will lead from there too.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Knowing vs. Knowing About
sessions.aim: To begin not with the doctrine of God but with the question underneath it, whether the point of theology was ever to be right about God or to be acquainted with him, and to face honestly that a person can master the facts of God for a lifetime and never once meet him, while refusing both the anti-intellectualism that despises study and the dead orthodoxy that mistakes study for the thing itself.
sessions.summary: We assume that to know God is to know a great deal about him, and so we read, we study, we accumulate, and we measure our nearness to God by the size of what we have collected. The first question of this whole study is whether that assumption is true, because there is a difference, J. I. Packer wrote about it in Knowing God in 1973, between knowing about a person and knowing the person, and it is the difference between reading a man's biography and sitting across a table from him. Bell takes the strong form of the worry. A study that opens by warning against too much head knowledge sounds like an excuse for laziness, a way to let people off the hook of hard thinking and call their ignorance humility. He grants the danger completely, because he came to faith through argument, through reading, through the hard work of being convinced, and he will not despise the very thing that brought him in. But the warning is not against knowing much. It is against stopping there. You can know that God is sovereign and never once have rested in it. You can be able to define the attributes and never have addressed the One who has them. The turn is this. Theology that never becomes prayer has not failed as theology. It has failed as theology's whole point, which was never information about God but communion with him. Knowing God begins where knowing about him bends its knee.

keyScripture.why: Jesus defines eternal life not as a place secured or a doctrine affirmed but as knowing God himself, that they know you the only true God and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, which makes acquaintance with God, not information about him, the very substance of salvation and the aim of all theology.

discussion.q: When you measure how close you are to God, what do you actually measure, how much you know, how you feel, how you behave, or something else, and what does that reveal about what you think knowing God means?
discussion.behind: Surface the working definition before any teaching. Most of us measure nearness to God by knowledge, feeling, or performance without ever examining the measure. The aim is to expose the assumption so the room can feel that knowing God might be something other than what they have been tracking. Land it on honesty, and go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Packer says there is a difference between knowing about a person and knowing the person. Can you name someone you know a great deal about but do not actually know, and someone you know but could not say much about, and what is the difference between the two?
discussion.behind: Move the distinction off the abstract and into ordinary relationship. Everyone has known a celebrity they cannot reach and a friend they cannot summarize. The aim is to feel the gap in a human case first, so that when it is applied to God it lands as something already understood rather than a theological trick.

discussion.q: Bell admits he came to faith through argument and reading and will not despise the very thing that brought him in. Where in your life has study of God been a real gift, and where has it become a substitute for actually coming to him?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves, because the session refuses to despise the mind. The aim is not to make people feel guilty for studying but to locate the precise point where good study quietly became a stopping place instead of a road. Affirm the learning, then press gently on where it went cold.

discussion.q: It is possible to know that God is good and never once have rested in it. Where is there a truth about God you could defend in a debate but have never let touch the part of you that is afraid or grieving?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap between the head and the rest of the person. We all hold doctrines we have never let reach the place that actually needs them. The aim is honest recognition of a specific truth held at arm's length, so the room feels why knowing about God is not the same as knowing him. Handle tenderly.

discussion.q: Bell says he has known a great deal about God on mornings when God himself felt completely absent. Where have you been able to recite the truth about God while feeling you did not know him at all, and what did you do with that?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to display it. You want each person, the leader included, inside the gap between knowing about God and knowing him, because that gap is exactly where this study means to do its work. Go first, and keep it gentle.

objections.objection: A study that opens by warning against head knowledge is just giving people permission to be lazy. You are dressing up ignorance as humility and telling people they do not need to think hard about God, which is exactly the excuse the shallow have always wanted.
objections.response: Sit inside this, because Bell agrees with more of it than you might expect, and he will not answer it from the safe side. He came to faith from atheism, and he came through thinking, through argument and reading and the slow work of being convinced against his will, so he will not despise the mind, and neither does this study. The warning is not against knowing much about God. It is against mistaking the knowing about for the knowing. A person can master the attributes of God and define every term correctly and still have never once addressed the One who has those attributes, the way a man can memorize a woman's biography and never have met her. That is not a call to read less. If anything it is a call to read better, to let the study become prayer rather than ending as a filed fact. Packer, who wrote one of the most rigorous popular books on the doctrine of God, was the one who insisted that the goal of all of it was to know God and not merely to know about him. The deepest thinkers in the church have always said this. The warning is not anti-intellectual. It is the intellect refusing to stop short of its own purpose.

objections.objection: If knowing God is about a personal acquaintance and not just information, then how is that different from the people who follow their feelings and call it God? You are making knowing God sound like an experience, and experiences lie.
objections.response: Fair, and the study guards exactly this, because a God known only by feeling is a God remade every time the feeling changes. Knowing God is not the warm experience set against the cold fact. It is both, in their right order. You cannot know a person you know nothing true about, so the facts are not optional, they are the content of the relationship, the actual truth about the actual God revealed in Scripture. But the facts were never the destination. They are the way in. Think of how you know anyone. You start with true things about them, their name, their history, their character, and those true things become the means by which you come to know not a profile but a person. The danger is not that we will know too many true things about God. It is that we will collect the true things and never let them carry us to him, the way a man might study a map of a country he never visits. The feeling, if it comes, is downstream of the truth, never a substitute for it. We are after a God known truly and known personally, and the one without the other is either a doctrine or a daydream.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If knowing God is not the same as knowing about him, and the difference is the difference between reading a man's biography and being known by him, which one have you actually been doing, and how long has it been since you came to him rather than studied him?
sessions.practice: This week, take one true thing you already know about God, that he is good, that he forgives, that he is near, anything you could already defend, and instead of studying it, pray it. Each day, take that one truth and say it back to God as an address, not a definition, telling him you know it and asking him to make it real to you and not merely true. Do not add new facts this week. Take the ones you have and walk them from your head to the One they are about, and write down at the end whether saying a known truth back to God as prayer felt different from holding it as information.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have studied you for years, some of us, and we are not sure we have met you. We have collected the true things and filed them, and called the filing a relationship. Forgive us for stopping at knowing about you when you offered us yourself. We do not despise the learning, you gave us minds and we will use them, but we confess we have let the learning become a place to hide from the One it was always about. Teach us the difference between reading your biography and being known by you. Take the truths we already hold and make them prayer. And to those of us who can recite you and have never rested in you, give the thing we cannot manufacture, not more about you, but you. In the name of Jesus, who came so that we might know you and not only know of you. Amen.
reflection: What have I been measuring when I measure my nearness to God, and is the thing I have been tracking actually knowing him, or only knowing about him?
Where is there a truth about God I could defend in an argument but have never let reach the part of me that is afraid, ashamed, or grieving?
If theology's whole point was communion and not information, what would change about how I read, study, and pray this week?
sessions.teaching: Start with the assumption almost all of us carry without examining it, that to know God is to know a great deal about him. We absorb this honestly. We are told the faith has content, that it matters what is true, that we should study, and all of that is right, and this study will not take a word of it back. So we read. We accumulate. We learn the attributes and the arguments and the doctrines, and somewhere along the way, quietly, we begin to measure our nearness to God by the size of what we have collected, as if the path to God were a stack of true sentences and the tallest stack stood closest. And the first question of this whole study, before we say one word about the Trinity, is whether that is true. Because there is a difference, and once you see it you cannot unsee it, between knowing about a person and knowing the person. J. I. Packer opened his book Knowing God, published in 1973, on exactly this distinction, and it is the hinge of everything that follows. I can know a great deal about a man, his birthplace, his history, his opinions, the shape of his life, and never have met him. I can read the biography of a stranger and close it knowing facts he himself has forgotten, and still, if he walked into the room, I would not know him and he would not know me. And I can know a person I could hardly describe, a friend whose biography I could not write, and yet know them, because I have sat across the table from them, because they know my name, because there is between us not information but acquaintance. That gap, between knowing about and knowing, is the gap this whole study lives in, and most of our religion lives on the wrong side of it. Now take the worry that rises immediately, because it is the honest one, and for some in the room it is more than theoretical. A study that opens by warning against head knowledge sounds like an excuse. It sounds like permission to be lazy, to read less, to dress up ignorance as humility and call the refusal to think hard a kind of spiritual maturity. I grant the danger, and I grant it without flinching, because I am the last person who gets to despise the mind. I did not drift into faith. I argued my way in, against my own resistance, out of atheism, through reading and thinking and the slow miserable work of being convinced of something I did not want to be true. The very thing that brought me in was the thing this objection is afraid I will now belittle, and I will not. Hear me clearly. The warning is not against knowing much about God. It is against stopping there. It is against the deadly assumption that once you have the facts you have the thing, when the facts were only ever the door. Packer himself wrote one of the most rigorous popular books on the doctrine of God ever written, hundreds of pages of careful theology, and the entire point of all that rigor, stated in his opening pages, was that we would come to know God and not merely to know about him. The deepest thinkers the church has produced are not the ones who said study less. They are the ones who refused to let study stop short of its own purpose. So this is not anti-intellectualism. This is the intellect, pressed to its end, discovering that its end was never itself. Let me say plainly what the problem looks like, because naming it is half the work. You can know that God is sovereign and never once have rested in his sovereignty on a night when everything was falling apart. You can be able to list the attributes, eternal, immutable, omnipotent, and never have addressed, in prayer, the One who is all of them. You can hold a doctrine of grace so precise you could defend it in a seminar and never have let it reach the part of you that is still ashamed of something done twenty years ago. The truth sits in the head, correct and cold, and the part of you that actually needed it, the frightened part, the grieving part, the part that lies awake, never gets the news. That is knowing about God. And I know it from the inside, because I have stood in front of people and taught the truth about God flawlessly on mornings when God himself felt utterly absent to me, when I could recite him and not find him, when the facts were all in place and the One the facts were about seemed to be in another country. If you have lived in that gap, you are not a bad Christian. You are most Christians, most of the time, and you are exactly the person this study is for. So here is the verdict that should land before we open a single page on the Trinity. Theology that never becomes prayer has not failed as theology. It has failed at theology's entire purpose. The reason to know that God is good is so that you will rest in his goodness. The reason to learn that he forgives is so that you will come to him forgiven. The reason to study the Trinity, which is where this whole study is going, is not to win an argument about the nature of God but to be drawn into the life of the God who is, eternally, a communion of love. Jesus said it as plainly as it can be said. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Not that they know about you. That they know you. Eternal life is not first a place you go. It is a Person you know. So we are going to spend five sessions on the highest and hardest doctrine the church holds, the one God in three persons, and I want to tell you at the outset what we are not doing. We are not solving a puzzle. We are not collecting a more impressive stack of true sentences. We are walking, slowly, from knowing about God toward knowing him, and the test of every session will not be whether you can now define the Trinity but whether the God we are studying has become, even a little, the God you actually address. The knowing about is not the enemy. It is the road. But a road you never walk down is just a line on a map. Knowing God begins the moment knowing about him bends its knee and turns the study into prayer.

scriptureStudy.note: And this is eternal life, that they know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God himself, not as information held or a place secured, which makes personal acquaintance with God the substance of salvation.

Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me. God himself ranks knowing him above wisdom, might, and riches, naming acquaintance with him as the only boast that holds.

I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. Paul, who knew more about God than almost anyone, treats all of it as loss next to knowing Christ personally, the scholar himself ranking acquaintance above information.

For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. God prefers being known to being served at a distance, which exposes the religion that performs for God without ever coming to him.

Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God. Paul warns that knowledge alone inflates, and locates the real thing in being known by God.

On that day many will say, did we not prophesy in your name, and then will I declare to them, I never knew you. The terrifying word is not that they knew too little about God but that he did not know them, the gap between knowing about and being known made final.

But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God. Paul corrects himself mid-sentence, because the deeper truth is not our knowing of God but God's knowing of us, the relationship grounded in his initiative, not our study.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian distinction between two kinds of knowledge of God, because it is older and more careful than the modern split between head and heart suggests. The medieval theologians distinguished knowledge that merely apprehends a truth from knowledge that rests in and loves the thing known, and the Reformers sharpened it further. John Calvin opened his Institutes, published in 1536, with the claim that there is no true knowledge of God that does not also produce reverence and love, that to know God rightly is to be moved by him, so that a knowledge of God which leaves the knower unchanged is not, by Calvin's account, real knowledge of God at all. Set this beside the modern academic ideal of detached, neutral knowledge, the posture that to know something truly you must hold it at arm's length and feel nothing, and ask whether that posture, useful as it is for studying rocks, can ever reach a Person. A serious group should weigh Packer's own framing in Knowing God, that the difference between knowing about God and knowing God is the difference that turns theology from a science into a relationship, and that the test of whether you know God is not the volume of what you can say about him but whether your knowledge has become praise, trust, and prayer. And weigh Augustine, who wrote in the Confessions that the heart is restless until it rests in God, naming the truth that the human mind was made not merely to grasp God as an object but to come to rest in him as its end. The discipline is to hold knowledge and communion together without collapsing either, refusing both the dead orthodoxy that knows everything about God and addresses him about nothing and the empty experience that feels much and knows nothing true, and to remember that the whole point of learning who God is, including the long and difficult doctrine we are about to study, was always that we would come to know him.

memoryVerse.text: And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

sessions.title: One God, Three Persons
sessions.aim: To state the doctrine of the Trinity carefully and historically, not as a riddle to be solved but as the church's confession of the God who is, and to see that God can be called love precisely because he was never alone, holding the doctrine as something received and confessed rather than something put up for the platform's vote.
sessions.summary: We come to the Trinity as if to a problem. One plus one plus one equals one, and that cannot be right, so either Christians cannot do arithmetic or they are hiding something. The first question is whether the Trinity was ever a math problem at all, or whether we have been reading it as the wrong kind of thing. Bell takes the strong form of the objection, that the doctrine is incoherent, a late invention forced on the simple monotheism of Jesus by councils centuries after him, three gods smuggled in under one name. He grants how it can look, and he grants that it cannot be drawn on a whiteboard without heresy. But the doctrine was not invented to complicate God. It was forced on the church by the data, by the refusal to give up either that there is one God, which Israel had bled to confess, or that Jesus and the Spirit are that God and not lesser things. The Council of Nicaea in 325 and the Council of Chalcedon in 451 did not vote God into being three. They drew the fence around a mystery the church had been worshiping from the start, ruling out the lies without claiming to exhaust the truth. Then the turn, and it is the heart of the session. If God were a solitary monad, alone for eternity past, then love would be something God learned only after he made someone to love, which means love would not be God's nature but his hobby. But the God who is eternally Father, Son, and Spirit was never alone. Love is not what God does. It is what God is, because God has been, forever, a communion. The Trinity is not the church's puzzle. It is the church's confession that the source of everything is, at its depth, self-giving love.

keyScripture.why: Jesus commands baptism into the name, singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, holding the oneness and the threeness together in a single breath, one name and three persons, which is the doctrine of the Trinity in the words of Jesus himself before any council ever met.

discussion.q: Be honest about how the Trinity has sat with you. Has it mostly felt like a math problem you could not solve, a doctrine you affirm but do not understand, or something you have genuinely worshiped, and why?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the real relationship people have with the doctrine, which is usually quiet bafflement or polite avoidance. The aim is to let the room admit the Trinity has been a riddle they tolerate rather than a God they adore, so the session can reframe it from problem to confession.

discussion.q: The doctrine was not invented to complicate God but forced on the church by two things it refused to surrender, that there is one God, and that Jesus and the Spirit are that God. Which of those two would you be tempted to give up to make the math easier, and what would be lost?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the pressure the early church felt. Every heresy was a way of relieving the tension by dropping one of the two truths. The aim is for people to feel that the doctrine is not arbitrary complexity but the only shape that keeps both non-negotiables, and to see what each shortcut costs.

discussion.q: Bell says the councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon did not vote God into being three but drew a fence around a mystery, ruling out the lies without claiming to exhaust the truth. How does it change the doctrine to hear it as a fence around a mystery rather than a full explanation of one?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the expectation that doctrine should explain God exhaustively. The creeds mark boundaries, saying not this and not that, more than they map the interior. The aim is to free people from thinking they have failed because they cannot fully comprehend the Trinity, since the church never claimed to either.

discussion.q: If God had been alone for eternity past, love would be something he learned only after making someone to love, a hobby and not his nature. What changes about God, and about you, if love is what God eternally is rather than something he later took up?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Press the room to feel the difference between a solitary God who learns to love and a God who is love because he was always communion. The aim is to feel that we are not loved as an afterthought of a lonely God but out of a love that has existed forever, which steadies the soul.

discussion.q: Bell admits he spent years treating the Trinity as a doctrine to defend rather than a God to adore, and could win the argument while never having worshiped the God he was defending. Where have you held a true thing about God as a position to defend rather than a Person to love?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. We can become defenders of orthodoxy who never worship the God orthodoxy describes. Go first and name it. The aim is honest recognition that being right about the Trinity is not the same as knowing the triune God, connecting this session back to session one.

objections.objection: The Trinity is just incoherent. One God who is three persons is one plus one plus one equals one, which is nonsense, and it was invented by councils three centuries after Jesus, who was a simple monotheist. You have smuggled three gods in under a single name.
objections.response: Bell grants two of the things buried in this, because they are true and pretending otherwise would weaken the answer. The Trinity cannot be drawn on a whiteboard without falling into heresy, and any neat diagram of it is wrong. And the formal language did come later, hammered out at Nicaea in 325 and refined at Chalcedon in 451. But hear what the councils did and did not do. They did not invent the Trinity. They were forced to it, against their own preference for simplicity, by data they would not surrender. Israel had died to confess that there is one God, and the church would not give that up. But the same church found itself worshiping Jesus as God, the Jesus who said before Abraham was, I am, who received worship, who forgave sins only God can forgive, and it experienced the Spirit as God, not as a force. They could not drop the oneness, and they could not drop the deity of the Son and the Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity is simply the refusal to lie about either. As for the math, it is only nonsense if God is three of the same thing he is one of. He is not. He is one in being and three in person, one what and three whos, which is not a contradiction but a category the modern mind, trained only on countable objects, has trouble holding. It is not three gods. It is the one God, who is, in his very depths, a fellowship.

objections.objection: Even if it is not three gods, the Trinity is impossible to understand, so why does it matter? Give me a God I can pray to. This abstract theology has nothing to do with my actual life, and I do not see why I should care whether God is one person or three.
objections.response: It matters more than almost anything, and the reason is the most practical thing in this whole study, so do not let the abstract language fool you. Here is what hangs on it. If God is a single, solitary person, alone before he made the world, then before there was anything to love, God did not love, because there was no one there. Love would be something God took up only after creation, a thing he does, not a thing he is. But the Bible says God is love, in his very being, eternally. That can only be true if God was never alone, if within the one God there has forever been a giving and receiving of love, the Father loving the Son in the Spirit, before a single creature existed. So when Scripture says God is love, it is not describing his mood. It is describing his nature, made possible only because he is three-in-one. And that changes your actual life completely, because it means you were not created by a lonely God who needed someone, and you are not loved as the solution to his solitude. You are invited into a love that was already full, already overflowing, already complete before you existed. A solitary god could only ever use you. The triune God can simply love you, because he was never short of it. There is no more practical truth than that.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the God who made you was never lonely, never short of love, complete in himself before you existed, then he did not create you out of need but out of overflow, so what would it mean to stop relating to God as someone you must keep satisfied and start receiving from a love that was always already full?
sessions.practice: This week, pray to the Trinity on purpose, which most of us never do. Each day, pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, naming all three, not as a formula but as a deliberate act of addressing the God who is actually three-in-one. Notice what you usually default to, a vague single deity, and instead come to the Father as a child, conscious that you come on the basis of what the Son has done, carried by the Spirit who prays in you. Do not try to understand the Trinity this week. Try to pray to it, and write down whether addressing God as Father, Son, and Spirit changed the texture of your prayer from talking at a force to coming to a fellowship.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, we confess we have treated you as a riddle when you are our salvation, a puzzle to tolerate when you are the fellowship of love that made and keeps us. We are sorry for the years we defended you without worshiping you. We could not have invented you, and we did not, you revealed yourself, one in being and three in person, and we receive it rather than vote on it. Thank you that you were never alone, that love is not something you learned but something you eternally are, and that you made us not out of need but out of overflow. Draw us, who are so often lonely, into the love you have had forever. We do not understand you. We adore you. Amen.
reflection: Have I been treating the Trinity as a math problem to solve or a God to worship, and what would it mean to receive it as confession rather than puzzle?
Which truth would I be tempted to drop to make God simpler, his oneness or the full deity of the Son and the Spirit, and what would I lose by dropping it?
If God was never lonely and made me out of overflow rather than need, how does that change the way I come to him, and the fear that I have to keep him satisfied?
sessions.teaching: We come to the Trinity as if we were walking up to a problem, and the problem looks like bad arithmetic. One God, three persons, and somewhere in the back of the mind a voice says that does not add up, one plus one plus one is three, not one, so either Christians cannot count or they are hiding something behind a word. And so for most of us the Trinity becomes a doctrine we affirm and avoid, something we recite in the creed and then set carefully on a high shelf, true, we suppose, but not something we expect to do anything. And the first question of this session is whether the Trinity was ever a math problem in the first place, or whether we have been reading it as the wrong kind of thing entirely. Take the objection at full strength, because it deserves it and because half-answering it is a kind of dishonesty. The charge is that the Trinity is simply incoherent, three gods smuggled in under a single name, and worse, that it was invented, that the simple monotheism of Jesus, a Jewish teacher who believed in one God, was overgrown centuries later by Greek-minded councils who voted a complicated doctrine into existence that Jesus would not have recognized. I want to grant what is true in this, because there is some, and conceding it costs the answer nothing. The Trinity genuinely cannot be diagrammed. Every neat picture of it, the three-leaf clover, the water-ice-steam, the man who is father and son and husband, every one of them, when pressed, collapses into a heresy the church already named and rejected. So if you have tried to draw it and failed, you have not failed at faith. You have discovered that it cannot be drawn, which the church knew before you. And it is true that the formal language, the precise vocabulary of one being and three persons, was hammered out later, at the Council of Nicaea in the year 325 and refined at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. So far the objection has its facts. But now watch what those councils actually did, because everything turns on it. They did not invent the Trinity. They were driven to it, reluctantly, by data they refused to surrender. Picture the position the early church was in. On one side, they were Jews, or taught by Jews, and the deepest confession of Israel, the one they had been killed rather than deny, was the Shema, hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. There is one God. That was not negotiable. It was the ground they stood on. But on the other side, those same monotheists found themselves doing something a strict monotheist should never do. They worshiped Jesus. This Jesus had said before Abraham was, I am, taking the divine name onto his own lips. He had forgiven sins, which everyone knew only God could do. He had received worship and not refused it, when every faithful Jew and every angel in Scripture refuses worship and redirects it to God alone. And after him, the same community experienced the Spirit not as an influence or a force but as God present, personal, to be obeyed and grieved and prayed to. So they were caught, held between two things they could not drop. One God. And Jesus and the Spirit are that God. Every heresy in the early centuries was, at bottom, an attempt to escape that tension by quietly letting go of one side of it. Some said Jesus was a created being, exalted but less than God, which saved the simple math at the cost of the deity of Christ, and that was the very thing Nicaea met in 325 to reject, confessing the Son to be of one being with the Father, true God from true God. Others collapsed the three into one God wearing three masks. The councils were not adding complexity for its own pleasure. They were drawing a fence, saying the mystery lives in here and these explanations out there are lies, not because we can map the interior but because we will not surrender either truth. That is what a creed is. It is less a full description of God than a fence around him, ruling out the falsehoods while leaving the mystery itself uncaptured. The church never claimed to comprehend the Trinity. Augustine, who wrote a massive work called On the Trinity over many years, said that if you think you have understood it, what you have understood is not God. The confession is not arrogance. It is the opposite. It is the refusal to flatten an infinite God into something a finite mind can fully hold. And the answer to the arithmetic is simply that God is not three of the same thing he is one of. He is one in being and three in person, one what and three whos. The contradiction only exists if you are counting the same category twice, and we are not. Three gods would be a contradiction. The one God who exists eternally as a fellowship of three persons is not a contradiction. It is a mystery, which is a different thing, a truth too large for the container, not a falsehood too broken to hold. But I have walked you through all of that, the councils and the categories, and I have to confess that I spent years doing exactly that and missing the entire point, because here is the heart of it, the thing that turns the Trinity from a doctrine you tolerate into a God you adore. Consider what it would mean if God were not three-in-one, if God were instead a single, solitary person, alone for all of eternity past before he made anything. The Bible says, plainly, that God is love. Not that God loves, though he does, but that God is love, in his very nature, eternally, before there was a world. Now think about what love requires. Love is not a thing you can do alone. Love is giving yourself to another, delighting in another, pouring out toward someone who is not you. So if God were solitary, alone before creation, then before he made the world there was no one for him to love, and love could not have been his nature. It would be something God learned, started doing only after he created someone to do it to. Love would be God's hobby, not God's self. And a God like that would have made the world out of need, to have someone, finally, to love, which would mean you and I exist to fill a void in God, loved the way a lonely man loves whoever finally walks into his empty house. But that is not the God revealed in Scripture, and the doctrine of the Trinity is precisely why. The one God has existed, forever, as Father, Son, and Spirit, in an unbroken communion of self-giving love, the Father loving the Son, the Son loving the Father, the Spirit the very bond and joy of that love, before a single star was made. God was never alone. God was never short of love. Which means love is not something God does. It is what God is, and it is what God is because God is three-in-one. And now feel what that does to your actual life, because this is the least abstract truth in the world. It means you were not created by a lonely God scraping together someone to love. You were created out of overflow, by a love that was already complete, already full, already pouring, that did not need you and made you anyway, simply to share what it already had. You are not the cure for God's solitude. You are the guest invited to a feast that was already going. A solitary god could only ever use you, lean on you, need you to make him whole. The triune God can simply love you, freely, without need, because he was never running low. There is no more steadying truth a frightened soul can hold. So here is the verdict this session leaves. The Trinity is not the church's embarrassing math problem, the doctrine we keep in the attic and bring down once a year. It is the church's confession that the source of everything, the ground under the whole universe, is not a force, not a solitary will, not a lonely power, but a communion, a fellowship, a Father and a Son and a Spirit who have loved each other forever and made a world to bring others in. I spent years able to win the argument and never once having worshiped the God I was defending. Do not make my mistake. We are not here to solve the Trinity. We are here to be drawn into it, because the God who is three-in-one made us for exactly that.

scriptureStudy.note: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The bedrock confession of Israel that there is one God, which the church refused to surrender, so that the Trinity is never three gods but always the one God of the Shema.

Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. One name, singular, and three persons named within it, the oneness and the threeness held together in a command of Jesus before any council met.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Word is both with God, distinct, and is God, the same in being, the grammar of the Trinity present in the first sentence of John's Gospel.

Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am. Jesus takes the divine name onto his own lips, claiming an eternal existence that belongs to God alone, which is why his hearers picked up stones, understanding the claim.
I and the Father are one. Jesus claims a unity with the Father that is more than agreement, a oneness of being, which the early church confessed at Nicaea as being of one substance with the Father.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Paul blesses the church in the name of all three persons together, an early and unselfconscious witness to the triune shape of God.

Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. God is not merely loving but is love in his nature, which can be true only of a God who was never alone, who has loved within himself eternally as Father, Son, and Spirit.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the work the church did to find language for the Trinity, because the precision was hard-won and the precision matters. The crisis that forced the issue came in the early fourth century, when a teacher named Arius argued that the Son was the highest of all created beings but still a creature, that there was a time when the Son was not. The Council of Nicaea in 325 met this directly, confessing the Son to be begotten, not made, of one being with the Father, the Greek term homoousios marking that the Son is the same in being as the Father and not a lesser thing made by him. Athanasius, who spent much of his life defending that confession at great personal cost, had argued in his earlier work On the Incarnation that only God can save, so that if the Son who saves us were not truly God, we would not in fact be saved, which is why the deity of Christ was never an abstract debate but the question of whether salvation is real. Set this beside the way the modern mind tends to treat all such distinctions as hairsplitting, and ask whether some truths are precise precisely because they are important, whether the difference between a Son who is God and a Son who is merely the greatest creature is the difference between being saved by God and being saved by something less. A serious group should weigh Augustine's On the Trinity, written over roughly two decades, in which he insists both that the doctrine is true and that it exceeds full comprehension, that the right response to the Trinity is not mastery but worship. And weigh the pastoral payoff that the Eastern church especially preserved, the idea that the persons of the Trinity exist in a mutual indwelling and self-giving, a communion so complete that to be saved is to be drawn into it. The discipline is to receive the doctrine as the church received it, as something confessed because revealed and not constructed because convenient, holding the oneness and the threeness without dropping either, and to let the careful language serve worship rather than replace it.

memoryVerse.text: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

sessions.title: The Father Who Runs
sessions.aim: To meet the first person of the Trinity not as a distant lawgiver but as the Father of Jesus' own parable, the one who runs toward the returning child, and to face honestly that for those whose earthly fathers failed them the word Father is the hardest word in the faith, while refusing both the sentimental picture of God and the bitter conclusion that the word means nothing.
sessions.summary: We have confessed the God who is three-in-one, and now we come to the first person of that fellowship, the Father, and the moment we say the word we hit a wall that no doctrine removes, because the word Father is not neutral. The first question is not what the fatherhood of God means in the abstract but what happens to a person whose own father walked out, or never came, or stayed only to wound, when they are told to call God Father. Bell takes the strong form of the wound, because he lived it. He was raised without a father, and he will not pretend the word is warm for everyone. He grants completely that for many in the room Father is a closed door and not an open arm. But the gospel does not respond to that wound by discarding the word, which leaves you praying to a force, and it does not respond by pretending your father was fine, which is a lie God never asked you to tell. It does something stranger. Jesus is not saying God is like your father. He is saying God is the Father your father was always a broken copy of, the original yours fell short of. And then the parable. The most famous father in all of literature is the father of the prodigal, who sees the ruined son a long way off and does the thing dignified fathers in that culture never did. He runs. Adoption, Paul says, makes the fatherless into sons who cry Abba, Father. The verdict is hard and tender at once. The first thing the gospel gives the fatherless is not advice but a Father, the original, who runs.

keyScripture.why: While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him, Jesus' own portrait of God the Father, who does not wait for the ruined child to grovel his way back but runs to meet him, which is the picture of the Father that overturns the distant or punishing one the wounded most fear.

discussion.q: When you hear God called Father, what is your honest first reaction, before the theologically correct one, and where do you think that reaction comes from?
discussion.behind: Surface the gut response before any teaching. For some the word is warm, for some it is a closed door, and the difference usually traces straight back to a human father. The aim is not to settle it but to expose it, because everyone in the room relates to whatever picture that word calls up. Land it on honesty, and go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell says God is not like your father, God is the Father your father was a broken copy of. What changes when you hear it that way around, the original instead of the echo?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge for the wounded. Many quietly assume God is their earthly father scaled up, which is terror for some. Help them feel the reversal, that the human father was the imperfect copy and God is the standard, so the failures of the one do not define the other. Handle tenderly.

discussion.q: In the parable the father runs, which fathers in that culture did not do, it was undignified. What does it do to your picture of God to see him running toward the ruined child rather than waiting with arms crossed for an apology?
discussion.behind: Press on the specific scandal of the parable. We assume God waits to be appeased. Jesus shows a father who abandons his dignity to reach the returning child first. The aim is to feel the warmth and the indignity of the running, which contradicts the distant or punishing father many fear God to be.

discussion.q: Adoption means the right to call God Father is not earned but given, a real new standing whether or not it feels true today. Where is it hardest for you to believe you are actually a child of God and not a tolerated outsider, and why?
discussion.behind: Get at the gap between the fact of adoption and the felt sense of it. Many believe in adoption as doctrine and live as orphans in practice, always trying to earn a place they have already been given. The aim is honest recognition of where they live as outsiders despite being sons and daughters.

discussion.q: Bell admits he came to God with no working picture of a good father and has prayed to a Father he could barely believe in. Where have you found the word Father hard, and what have you done with that difficulty?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. You are not hunting for painful confession to display it. You want each person, the leader included, inside the difficulty, because the gospel gives a Father precisely to those who never had one. Go first, and keep it gentle, and protect anyone for whom this is fresh.

objections.objection: Calling God Father is fine for people who had good fathers. For the rest of us it is a cruelty. You are asking me to feel safe with the very word that names the person who hurt me most, and no doctrine fixes that.
objections.response: Sit inside this, because Bell does, and he will not answer it from a safe distance. He was raised without a father. He knows the word can land like a wound and not a comfort, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. So hear the distinction with care. Jesus is not saying God is a bigger version of your father. He is saying the reverse. God is the Father, the real and original one, and every earthly father, the absent one and the cruel one and even the good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken copy at that. Your father did not define fatherhood and then God had to live up to it. God defined it, and your father fell short. So when you call God Father, you are not handing God the face of the man who failed you. You are appealing past that man to the One he was supposed to image and did not. And then look at what kind of Father this actually is. Jesus did not describe him as a stern judge tapping his foot. He told a story about a father who saw his wrecked, disgraced son a long way off and ran, lost his dignity, threw his arms around the ruin of a boy before a word of apology was out. That is the Father the word belongs to. It does not belong to your wound. It belongs to him, and he is giving it to you.

objections.objection: If God is such a good Father, why did he let me grow up without one? You are offering me a heavenly Father as if that erases the human father I needed and never had, and it does not. The hole is still there.
objections.response: Bell will not wave this away, because the hole is real and he carries the same one, and a heavenly Father does not retroactively give you the childhood you should have had. So hear what the gospel does and does not claim. It does not claim the wound never happened or that it does not matter, and it does not promise that knowing God as Father makes the ache of the absent one disappear. What it claims is harder and truer. It says there was always supposed to be a Father, that your longing for one was not a defect or a weakness but the right instinct aimed at the right thing, that you were made by and for a Father and the hunger you feel is the shape of what you were made for. The absence you grew up with was real, and it was wrong, and God does not bless it or excuse it. But the longing underneath the absence was pointing somewhere true the whole time. The gospel does not erase the empty chair. It tells you there is a Father who was always meant to fill it, who runs toward you now, and who will, in the end, wipe every tear, including that one. The hole is not denied. It is, slowly, met.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God really is the Father your earthly father was only a broken copy of, and he runs toward the ruined child rather than waiting to be appeased, what is the one thing you have always needed a father to do or say, and have never had, that this Father is running to give you?
sessions.practice: This week, read the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15 slowly, every day, and each time stop at the verse where the father runs, and stay there. Do not rush to the lesson. Picture yourself as the returning child and God as the one running, and notice what rises in you, whether it is hope, or disbelief, or a flinch, and do not judge what comes. Then, once this week, address God out loud as Father, even if the word is hard, even if you have to say it like a child learning a name he never got to use, and tell him honestly where the word is difficult for you. Write down whether seeing God as the Father who runs changed how you came to him.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us say that word easily and some of us say it with a clenched jaw, because the man it should have named left, or never came, or stayed and did damage. You know which of us is which. We thank you that you are not the echo of our earthly fathers but the original they failed to copy, and that you are not the stern judge waiting to be appeased but the Father who runs, who saw the ruined child a long way off and could not wait. To the fatherless among us, and we are more of us than we admit, give the staggering news that they have a Father, the real one, the original, who has been running toward them the whole time they were sure no one was coming. Make us your children, not because we earned it, but because you ran. In the name of Jesus, your Son, who showed us your face. Amen.
reflection: What picture of a father do I bring to God without realizing it, and how has that picture shaped the way I relate to him, or kept me from him at all?
Where have I assumed God is my earthly father scaled up, when the gospel says my earthly father was only ever a broken copy of him?
If I am truly adopted, a child of God whether or not it feels true today, and the Father runs toward the returning child, what would change about how I come to him this week?
sessions.teaching: We have spent a session confessing the God who is three-in-one, the eternal fellowship of Father, Son, and Spirit, and now we come down into that fellowship to meet the first person of it, the Father, and the instant we say the word we run into something no doctrine can smooth over. The word Father is not neutral. It is the most loaded word in the faith. For some of you it is the warmest word there is, because behind it stands a man who was present, who was kind, who was strong and gentle in the right measure, and when you hear God called Father, something in you relaxes. But for others of you, and I am one of them, the word is not a warm room. It is a locked door. Behind it stands a man who left, or who never appeared at all, or who appeared only to wound, and to be told to call God Father is to be told to feel safe with the very name that taught you men cannot be trusted to stay. So before we say one more sentence about the fatherhood of God in the abstract, we have to be honest about what that word does to the people actually in the room. I was raised without a father. I came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith and no working picture of what a good father even was, so when I tell you I understand the flinch, I am not performing sympathy from a safe distance. I am telling you my own. And I will not do the thing the church too often does, which is to wave the wound away, to rush past it to the comforting doctrine as if the pain were an inconvenience to the lesson. The pain is not an inconvenience. For a great many people it is the single biggest obstacle between them and God, and it deserves to be named, not managed. So let us take the hardest form of the objection seriously, because it is the honest one. Calling God Father, the objection says, is a comfort if you had a good father and a cruelty if you did not. You are asking the wounded to find safety in the exact word that names their deepest injury, and no amount of theology repairs that. I grant the weight of it entirely. But the objection misses something, and it is everything, and getting the direction of it right is the whole turn of this session. Jesus is not saying God is like your father. That is the lie that terrifies the wounded, the quiet assumption that God is simply your earthly father scaled up to cosmic size, the same absence and the same temper with infinite power behind it now. Jesus is saying the exact opposite, and you have to hear which way it runs. God is the Father. The original. The real one. And every human father who ever lived, the one who left and the one who stayed and even the rare good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken copy at that. Your father did not set the standard for fatherhood that God then had to meet. God set the standard, and your father fell short of it, the way every image falls short of the original it was made from. This is not word play, and it is not a trick to make you feel better. It is the reversal the fatherless need most, because it means that when you call God Father, you are not addressing the man who failed you with a bigger title. You are appealing past him, over his head, to the One he was supposed to show you and did not. The word does not belong to your wound. It belongs to God. And then the question becomes, what kind of Father is the original, and here Jesus does not hand us a definition. He tells us a story, the most famous story about a father ever told. A son demands his inheritance early, which in that culture was a way of saying to his father, I wish you were dead, and then takes the money and burns it all in a far country until he is starving in a pig field, which for a Jewish boy is as low and unclean as the story can put him. And he decides to go home, not hoping to be a son again, that door he is sure is closed, but hoping only to be hired as a servant, and he rehearses his apology on the long road back. Now listen to what the father does, because every detail is chosen to overturn what we assume about God. The father has been watching the road. While the son is still a long way off, still a speck on the horizon, still rehearsing his speech, the father sees him, and Scripture says he felt compassion, and ran. You have to understand what that meant. A dignified man of standing in that culture did not run. Running required gathering up your robes and exposing your legs, an indignity beneath a man of honor. And this father, seeing the ruin of his boy in the distance, throws his dignity to the wind and runs, in front of the whole village, to reach his disgraced son before the son can even finish the apology, and throws his arms around him and kisses him while the boy still smells of the pigs. That is the Father the word belongs to. Not the stern judge with arms crossed, waiting for the groveling to reach the right pitch before he decides whether to relent. A Father who is already watching the road, who runs, who reaches the child first, who interrupts the apology with an embrace. If your picture of God the Father is the foot-tapping disciplinarian waiting to be appeased, Jesus is telling you, with this story, that you have the wrong father in mind. The right one is undignified with love. And what makes this yours and not just a nice story is a word the New Testament uses, adoption. Paul writes that we have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. Adoption is a legal act, a deliberate decision to take someone who was not your child and make them your child, with all the standing and inheritance of one born into the house. It is not a metaphor stretched thin. It is a real new status, and the staggering thing about it, the thing that should stop the fatherless in their tracks, is that adoption is, by definition, for those who did not have a father. You do not adopt your own children. You adopt the ones who had no place, and that is precisely the word God uses for what he does. He takes the fatherless and makes them sons and daughters, gives them the family name, the inheritance, the right to come into his presence and call him not Lord, not Judge, not Sir, but Abba, the most intimate word a child has for a father. And here is where I have to step inside this rather than stand outside it, because I am not teaching this from the far shore of having figured it out. I came to God with no working picture of a good father, and there were years when I prayed to a Father I could barely believe in, saying the word with a part of me bracing for him to be like the absence I had known. The fact of my adoption was true on those mornings whether or not it felt true, and slowly, slowly, the running Father in the story began to overtake the absent father in my history, not by erasing the wound but by being, simply, real, and present, and unlike the man I had feared he would be. So here is the verdict this session leaves, and it is hard and tender in the same breath. The first thing the gospel gives the fatherless is not a technique for healing and not advice for coping. It is a Father. The original, the real one, the standard every earthly father was only a shadow of, who does not wait at a distance to be appeased but watches the road and runs. If you came tonight carrying the empty chair, the father who left or never came, hear this and let it land. There was always supposed to be a Father. The hunger you have carried your whole life is not a defect. It is the shape of the thing you were made for, and it is being answered, not by a heavenly version of the man who failed you, but by the One he was always meant to point you to and could not. Say the word, even if you have to say it like a child learning a name he never got to use. The Father is already running.

scriptureStudy.note: While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. Jesus' own picture of God the Father, who runs toward the returning child, undignified with love, the opposite of the distant or punishing father many fear.

You received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The right to call God Father is not natural but given in adoption, and the Spirit himself prompts the cry, so even the word in our mouths is grace, not achievement.

God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The intimacy is the Spirit's work, not our accomplishment, which means the fatherless can call God Father truly because it is God's Spirit, not our history, that supplies the word.

A father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. Long before Jesus, God claimed the title precisely for those who had no father, which tells you the name was always aimed at the ones who needed it most.

See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God, and so we are. Adoption is not a metaphor stretched thin but a real new standing, named by the Father himself over those who had none.

If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him. Jesus argues from the broken copy to the original, the imperfect human father pointing to a Father immeasurably better.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. The Father is not finally unknown or guessed at, he has a face, the face of the Son, so that the Father we are invited to call our own is the one we see in Jesus.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the recovery of the doctrine of adoption, because the modern reflex to call everyone a child of God in the same sense quietly empties the word of the very thing that makes it precious to the fatherless. The Reformers and the Puritans treated adoption as one of the high points of salvation, not merely that the sinner is forgiven and acquitted, which is justification, but that the forgiven one is then brought into the family and given the standing of a son or daughter, with the inheritance and the intimacy that belong to a child. J. I. Packer, in Knowing God, made the striking claim that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel offers, higher even than justification, because to be justified is to be declared righteous before a judge, but to be adopted is to be received into the embrace of a Father, and a good father is more than a just judge. Set this beside the sentimental modern assumption that everyone everywhere is automatically God's child by nature, and ask what is gained and what is lost in the flattening. The older view took adoption seriously as a gift deliberately given, which made the word Father precious rather than generic, the costly act of a Father who chose the fatherless. A serious group should weigh the pastoral edge here, because this is where the doctrine meets the wound. For those raised without a father, adoption is not an abstraction but the very thing they most lacked and most longed for, and the gospel offers it not as a consolation prize but as the center, a Father deliberately given to those who had none, which is exactly why Psalm 68 calls God the father of the fatherless before the New Testament ever opens. And weigh the parable of the prodigal as Jesus' own commentary on the Father's character, the running father who reaches the child first, against every picture of God as the distant lawgiver who must be appeased. The discipline is to hold the word Father as both holy and tender, neither so reverent it goes cold nor so familiar it goes cheap, and to remember that for many in the room it is the most contested and the most longed-for word in the faith.

memoryVerse.text: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

sessions.title: The Son Who Reveals
sessions.aim: To see that the God who could have remained forever unknown made himself known in the Son, the exact imprint of his nature, so that to have seen Jesus is to have seen the Father, and to hold the full deity and humanity of Christ as the church's confession, stated pastorally, against both the reduction of Jesus to a great teacher and the abstraction of God into an unknowable cloud.
sessions.summary: We have met the Father, but a question hangs over the whole study, the oldest religious problem there is, whether God can finally be known at all or whether he is, in the end, a cloud, a mystery, a silence we project our guesses onto. The first question is whether God is finally hidden or whether he has shown his face. Bell takes the strong form of the agnostic's honesty, that every religion claims to know God and they cannot all be right, that the safest and most honest position is that the infinite is beyond us and anyone who claims to know what God is like is overreaching. He grants the integrity of that, and he grants that apart from revelation it would be the wise conclusion. But the Christian claim is not that we reasoned our way up to God. It is that God came down. The letter to the Hebrews calls the Son the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and Colossians calls him the image of the invisible God. Jesus himself, when asked to show the Father, said whoever has seen me has seen the Father. The turn is the most important sentence in the study. God is not finally unknown. The infinite did not stay a cloud. He took a face, a voice, a set of hands, a way of treating lepers and children and the woman caught in adultery, and that face is the face of God. If you want to know what God is like, you do not guess, and you do not climb. You look at Jesus. The Son is not a window onto a God who remains hidden behind him. The Son is God, made visible, so that the unknowable became, in him, the most known person who ever lived.

keyScripture.why: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, naming the Son not as a messenger pointing toward a hidden God but as the precise expression of God's own being, so that in Jesus the invisible God has made himself exactly and reliably visible, and is no longer finally unknown.

discussion.q: Be honest about your working assumption. Deep down, do you suspect God is finally unknowable, a mystery we only guess at, or do you believe he has actually made himself known, and how does that assumption shape your faith?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the quiet agnosticism many believers carry, the sense that God is ultimately a cloud we hope about. The aim is to name that assumption so the session can confront it with the claim that God has taken a face, which is either true or it is not, and the difference is enormous.

discussion.q: The claim of the faith is not that we reasoned our way up to God but that God came down. How is being shown God in a person different from concluding things about God by argument, and why does it matter which one Christianity is?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the difference between revelation and speculation. Most religious thinking is a climbing up toward God by reason. Christianity claims a coming down. The aim is to feel that we are not guessing about God's character from a distance but reading it off an actual life, which is a different kind of knowing entirely.

discussion.q: Jesus said whoever has seen me has seen the Father. If that is true, then the way Jesus treated people, lepers, children, the woman caught in adultery, is the way God treats people. Where does that picture of God differ from the God you secretly fear he might be?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap between the God of our fears and the God with a face. Many carry a default image of God as harsher than Jesus. The aim is to let the actual conduct of Jesus correct the feared God, so people feel that God is exactly as kind, and exactly as demanding, as Jesus was, and not secretly otherwise.

discussion.q: If the Son is the exact imprint of God's nature and not merely a great teacher pointing beyond himself, then everything about God hangs on who Jesus is. Why is it not enough to call Jesus a wise man or a good example, and what is lost if that is all he was?
discussion.behind: Hold the confessional line pastorally. The reduction of Jesus to a great teacher is the most common modern move and it quietly empties the gospel. The aim is for the room to see that if Jesus is only a teacher, God remains unknown, and that the deity of Christ is what makes God knowable, not optional theological decoration.

discussion.q: Bell admits he wanted, as a skeptic, a God he could keep abstract and at a distance, and that a God with a face is harder to avoid than a God who stays a cloud. Where would you rather keep God vague, and what does a God with an actual face ask of you that a cloud does not?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. A vague God makes no claim, a God with a face does. Go first and name where you prefer God abstract. The aim is honest recognition that a knowable God is also an unavoidable one, that revelation is a gift and also a summons we cannot easily dodge.

objections.objection: Every religion claims to know what God is like, and they all disagree, so the honest position is that God, if there is one, is beyond all of us, and anyone who says they know his character is overreaching. Why should the Christian claim about Jesus be different from anyone else's guess?
objections.response: Bell grants the integrity of this, because it is the honest agnostic position and he held something close to it himself, and he agrees that if knowing God were a matter of us reasoning our way up to the infinite, the humble conclusion would indeed be that we cannot, that the cloud is too high and our guesses are just guesses. But notice that the Christian claim is not that kind of claim at all. It is not we climbed up and figured God out. It is God came down and showed us. The difference is everything. One is speculation about a distant object, the other is revelation by a personal subject who chose to be seen. You do not arrive at the Christian picture of God by inference, by reasoning from the world to its cause and guessing at the character behind it. You arrive at it by looking at a particular man who lived at a particular time and did particular things, and hearing him say that to see him is to see the Father. That is a testable kind of claim in a way a cloud is not, because it has a face and a record. You can read what he was like, how he treated the outcast and the child and the guilty, and ask whether that is the character of God. The claim is not that we are sure we guessed right. It is that we stopped guessing, because God walked into the room. You are free to reject that he did. But it is not the same kind of claim as a guess about a cloud, and treating it as one misses what is actually being said.

objections.objection: I can admire Jesus as a great moral teacher, maybe the greatest, without believing he was God. Why is that not enough? It seems like you are taking a wise man and inflating him into a deity to prop up a doctrine.
objections.response: It is a reasonable place to want to stop, and many sincere people stop there, so hear why the faith cannot. If Jesus was only a great teacher, then God remains exactly as unknown as he was before, because a great teacher can tell you things about God but cannot be the showing of God, and the whole Christian claim is not that Jesus described the Father well but that to see him is to see the Father, which only makes sense if he is the exact imprint of God's nature and not a gifted commentator on it. And there is a harder problem with the wise-teacher-only position, which is that the wise teacher said things no merely wise teacher should say. He forgave sins, which everyone present knew only God could do. He accepted worship. He claimed to have existed before Abraham, taking the divine name onto his lips. A merely wise man who said those things would not be wise, he would be deluded or dishonest, so the calm great-teacher Jesus the objection wants to keep is not actually available in the record, the record gives us a man making claims a good teacher does not make. The faith did not inflate a wise man into God. It received a man who claimed to be God and backed the claim with a resurrection, and then spent centuries finding careful language for what he plainly was. You can deny the resurrection and the claims. But the gentle moral-teacher-only Jesus is not a real option in the texts, he is a figure we construct by editing out everything inconvenient he said.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God is not finally a cloud but has shown his face in Jesus, and the way Jesus treated the guilty and the outcast and the child is exactly the way God treats you, then who have you been imagining God to be that the actual face of Jesus would correct, and are you willing to let the real one replace the feared one?
sessions.practice: This week, read one of the Gospels, or a long stretch of one, with a single question in front of you, what is God like, on the conviction that whatever Jesus is like, God is exactly like. Watch how he treats the people everyone else wrote off, the leper he touched, the child he welcomed, the woman caught in the act whom no one expected him to spare, and each time, instead of saying that is how Jesus is, say that is how God is. Do not study it as a moral lesson. Read it as a portrait of the Father, made visible in the Son. Write down where the God you saw in Jesus differed from the God you had been quietly imagining, and what it would mean to trust the real one.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have spent our lives, some of us, suspecting you were finally a cloud, a mystery we could only guess at, and keeping you vague because a vague God asks nothing of us. We thank you that you did not stay hidden. You did not leave us climbing and guessing. You came down, and you took a face, and the face is the face of Jesus, the radiance of your glory, the exact imprint of your nature, so that we no longer have to wonder what you are like. Forgive us for preferring you abstract, and for fearing you were harsher than your Son. Teach us to read the kindness and the holiness of Jesus as your own, to know that whoever has seen him has seen you. You are not unknown. You have a face. Let us look at it, and find you there. In the name of the Son who showed us the Father. Amen.
reflection: Do I secretly believe God is finally unknowable, a cloud I only guess at, and how would my faith change if I truly believed he has shown his face in Jesus?
Where is the God I fear harsher, or colder, or more distant than the Jesus of the Gospels, and what would it mean to let the actual face of Christ correct the God of my fears?
If calling Jesus merely a great teacher leaves God unknown, what do I actually believe about who Jesus is, and have I let that be the foundation of how I know the Father?
sessions.teaching: We have met the Father, the running Father of the parable, and now a question hangs over the whole study that we have to face directly, because it is the oldest religious problem there is and most believers carry a quiet version of it without ever saying it out loud. Can God actually be known? Or is he, in the end, a cloud, an infinite mystery, a silence onto which every religion projects its best guesses, so that all our confident statements about what God is like are really just educated speculation dressed up as knowledge? This is not only the skeptic's question. It lives inside the church too, in the believer who affirms the doctrines but suspects, underneath, that God himself is ultimately unreachable, that we have words about him but not him, that the divine is finally hidden and we are all, however devout, just hoping in the dark. So the first question of this session is the plainest and the largest. Is God finally hidden, or has he shown his face? Let me take the strong form of the agnostic position, because it is the honest one and it deserves more respect than the church usually gives it. The agnostic says, look, every religion on earth claims to know what God is like, and they flatly contradict each other, and they cannot all be right. The God of one is wrathful, of another serene, of another many, of another a force. Given that, the humble and honest conclusion is that the infinite is beyond all of us, that a being big enough to be God is by definition bigger than any human mind can map, and that anyone who tells you confidently what God is like has overreached, has mistaken their guess for knowledge. I want to grant the integrity of that, fully, because I held a version of it myself, and because it is, in fact, exactly the right conclusion, if you start where the agnostic starts. If knowing God is a matter of us reasoning our way up to him, climbing from the world we can see toward the infinite we cannot, then yes, the cloud is too high, the gap is too wide, and our best theology is just our best guessing.
